A stored procedure call

questions.q: What makes a subquery a 'scalar' or single-value subquery?
options: It is guaranteed to return exactly one value
It can only reference one column
It never uses WHERE
It must always use GROUP BY
questions.explain: Scalar subqueries collapse to exactly one value, most often via an aggregate function.

questions.q: What happens if a scalar subquery unexpectedly returns more than one row?
options: SQL Server raises a runtime error
It silently uses only the first row
It silently uses only the last row
It averages all the returned rows automatically
questions.explain: SQL Server has no defined way to compare a single value against multiple results in this context, so it errors out.

questions.q: Why do scalar subqueries almost always wrap an aggregate function?
options: Aggregate functions are guaranteed to collapse to exactly one value
Aggregate functions are required syntax for any subquery
It's purely a style convention with no functional reason
Non-aggregate subqueries are not allowed in T-SQL
questions.explain: Using AVG, COUNT, MAX, MIN, or SUM guarantees the single-value requirement is met.

questions.q: Where can a scalar subquery be used in a query?
options: Anywhere a single value is expected — in WHERE, in a SELECT column, or standing in for a literal
Only inside a WHERE clause
Only inside a JOIN's ON clause
Only as the very first statement in a script
questions.explain: Since it evaluates to one value, it's valid anywhere a literal or expression producing one value would be valid.
